skills.name: Approximate numbers: place value, rounding, rounding up and down

note.text:
The value of a digit depends on its place: in 3.4567 the 5 stands for 5 hundredths, 0.05.
To round, look at the next digit: 5 or more, round up; 4 or less, keep.
• 3.4567 to 1 decimal place: 3.5. To 2 decimal places: 3.46. To the nearest whole number: 3.
• 4 682 to the nearest hundred: 4 700.
In real problems you sometimes must round up (buses needed for 130 pupils, 50 per bus: 3) or down (full boxes of 12 from 130 eggs: 10), whatever the next digit is.
A rounded value has bounds: 4.7 to 1 d.p. means 4.65 ≤ x < 4.75.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to give the value of any digit, round to a number of decimal places or to the nearest {10}, {100}, {1000}, and decide when to round up or down.
Builds on: Form One place value and rounding.
Leads to: Lessons {33} and {34} (significant figures, errors and bounds) and every measured answer in science.

sections.heading: Place value and rounding
sections.text:
In {3.4567}: {3} units, {4} tenths, {5} hundredths, {6} thousandths, {7} ten-thousandths. The {5} stands for {0.05}.
To round, keep the digits you need and look at the next one:
• {3.4567} to {1} d.p.: next digit {5} → {3.5}.
• to {2} d.p.: next digit {6} → {3.46}.
• {4682} to the nearest {100}: next digit {8} → {4700}.
Keep the size: {4682} to the nearest {100} is {4700}, not {47}.

sections.heading: Up, down and bounds
sections.text:
Sometimes the meaning decides, not the digit:
• {130} pupils, {50} per bus: {130} ÷ {50} = {2.6}, but {2} buses leave pupils behind: {3} buses.
• {130} eggs, boxes of {12}: {10.8}, but only {10} boxes are full.
A rounded value stands for a range. {4.7} to {1} d.p. could be anything from {4.65} up to just below {4.75}: half a unit each way. These are its lower and upper bounds.

key_words.meaning: go to the next value above / below
the smallest and largest values that round to a given number

mistake.why: Rounding keeps the size of the number: fill the places with zeros.

worked_example.problem: {n} pupils travel on buses that each carry {c}. How many buses are needed?
steps: {floor(n / c)} buses carry only {floor(n / c) * c} pupils; the others still need a seat.

cards.idea: Rounding: look at the next digit. {5} or more, round up; less than {5}, keep.
In a problem, decide whether to round up or down from the meaning.
example: {130} pupils, {50} per bus: {3} buses (up). {130} eggs, boxes of {12}: {10} full boxes (down)

check.prompt: {up ? n + ' people need transport in vans that carry ' + c + ' each. How many vans are needed?' : 'Mangoes are packed ' + c + ' to a crate. How many full crates can be made from ' + n + ' mangoes?'}
check.answer: up ? floor((n + c - 1) / c) : floor(n / c)

misconceptions.explain: {up ? 'Rounding down leaves people behind' : 'A part-filled crate is not full'}: round {up ? 'up' : 'down'}.
misconceptions.when: round(n / c) != (up ? floor((n + c - 1) / c) : floor(n / c))

solution: {up ? 'Everyone needs a seat, so round up' : 'Only full crates count, so round down'}.
where: round(n / c) == (up ? floor(n / c) : floor((n + c - 1) / c))

cards.idea: A rounded number stands for a range: half a unit either side.
example: {4.7} to {1} d.p.: from {4.65} up to (not including) {4.75}

check.prompt: A length is {fmt(x)} cm, correct to {1} decimal place. Which range contains the true length L?

misconceptions.explain: Go half a unit each way: {0.05}, not {0.1}.
Rounding works both ways: values just below {fmt(x)} also round to it.
The accuracy is {1} d.p., so the half-unit is {0.05}.

solution: To {1} d.p. the unit is {0.1}; half of it is {0.05}.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the digit {dig} in {fmt(x)}?

misconceptions.explain: {dig} is not in the units place: it stands for {dig} ÷ {10 ^ pos}.
Places after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths: divide, do not multiply.
The next digit is {k == 1 ? d2 : d3}, so round up.
Count the decimal places carefully: {k} place{k == 1 ? '' : 's'} after the point.

solution: It is {k == 1 ? d2 : d3}: {(k == 1 ? d2 : d3) >= 5 ? 'round up' : 'keep'}.

misconceptions.explain: Keep the size of the number: write the zeros, {roundTo(n, u)}.

solution: Look at the digit after the {u == 10 ? 'tens' : u == 100 ? 'hundreds' : 'thousands'} place.
